kbl2 <- function(x, ...) kable(x, align = "lrrrrrr", ...) |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

1 Overview

Last time we built neural networks with neuralnet, keras, and torch, but we never really leaned on two things that matter in practice: regularization, and architectures beyond a stack of dense layers. This document does both, entirely in torch:

  1. Same complexity level as before, but regularized. We refit a small network on a familiar tabular dataset (Framingham), this time comparing an unregularized version against one with dropout and weight decay (L2 regularization via the optimizer).
  2. A genuinely harder problem. We build our first real convolutional neural network (CNN) on real medical images — chest X-rays, predicting pneumonia — rather than the flattened-pixel MLP we used for MNIST.

2 Part 1: Tuning and Regularizing a Small Network

Neural networks come with many choices: how many hidden layers, how many units per layer, how much dropout, how much weight decay, and how fast to learn. Rather than guess, we’ll do this the way we’ve done model selection all semester, with an honest three-way split:

Set Used for
Training (60%) fitting the network weights
Validation (20%) comparing architectures/hyperparameters, choosing the best model, and choosing a classification threshold
Test (20%) one final, honest estimate of performance — touched only at the very end

2.1 Data

We reuse the Framingham data from earlier in the course, predicting TenYearCHD from a handful of predictors.

framingham <- read_csv("framingham.csv") |>
  select(TenYearCHD, age, male, currentSmoker, prevalentHyp, diabetes,
         totChol, sysBP, BMI, heartRate, glucose) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    TenYearCHD = factor(TenYearCHD, levels = c(0, 1)),
    male          = factor(male),
    currentSmoker = factor(currentSmoker),
    prevalentHyp  = factor(prevalentHyp),
    diabetes      = factor(diabetes)
  )

2.2 Is This a Good Problem for a Neural Network?

Reasons it might be:

  • Networks can learn nonlinear effects and interactions automatically, without us specifying them as we would in a logistic regression.
  • The problem is small, so we can afford to tune many architectures.

Reasons it might not be:

  • Small, low-dimensional tabular data. We have ~2,500 training rows and 10 predictors. Neural networks tend to shine with very large samples and/or high-dimensional, unstructured inputs (images, text, signals). On modest tabular data, random forests, boosting, and even plain logistic regression are usually as good or better, and much easier to tune.
  • Weak signal. Ten-year CHD risk is only partly predictable from these measurements, so the achievable AUC is modest (roughly 0.70 to 0.75). When the ceiling is that low, a fancier model has little room to help. That’s why the many network configurations above land within noise of each other, and why the random forest is in the same ballpark.
  • Tuning burden and interpretability. The network has many knobs (architecture, dropout, weight decay, learning rate, epochs, seed) and is much harder to explain to a clinician than a logistic regression or a single tree.

The takeaway isn’t that neural networks are bad, but that they should have to earn their place against simpler benchmarks. Here the network edges out the random forest by a few points of AUC, but the difference is small relative to the noise, and the smallest network (8 units) won, which says the extra flexibility isn’t buying much. Part 2 is a much better fit.

2.3 Preprocessing

set.seed(2026)
split1    <- initial_split(framingham, prop = 0.6, strata = TenYearCHD)
train_raw <- training(split1)
holdout   <- testing(split1)

split2    <- initial_split(holdout, prop = 0.5, strata = TenYearCHD)
val_raw   <- training(split2)
test_raw  <- testing(split2)

# preprocessing is learned on the training set only, then applied to all three
rec <- recipe(TenYearCHD ~ ., data = train_raw) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

prep_rec <- prep(rec)
train <- bake(prep_rec, train_raw)
val   <- bake(prep_rec, val_raw)
test  <- bake(prep_rec, test_raw)

c(train = nrow(train), validation = nrow(val), test = nrow(test))
     train validation       test 
      2296        765        766

2.4 Torch Tensors and Dataloaders

to_x <- function(d) torch_tensor(as.matrix(select(d, -TenYearCHD)), dtype = torch_float())
# torch's cross-entropy loss wants class indices starting at 1
to_y <- function(d) torch_tensor(as.integer(d$TenYearCHD), dtype = torch_long())

x_train_t <- to_x(train); y_train_t <- to_y(train)
x_val_t   <- to_x(val);   y_val_t   <- to_y(val)
x_test_t  <- to_x(test);  y_test_t  <- to_y(test)

# outcomes coded 0/1 for yardstick
y_train <- as.integer(train$TenYearCHD) - 1
y_val   <- as.integer(val$TenYearCHD)   - 1
y_test  <- as.integer(test$TenYearCHD)  - 1

train_dl <- dataloader(tensor_dataset(x_train_t, y_train_t), batch_size = 64, shuffle = TRUE)
val_dl   <- dataloader(tensor_dataset(x_val_t,   y_val_t),   batch_size = 64, shuffle = FALSE)

n_features <- ncol(x_train_t)
n_features
[1] 10

2.5 A Flexible Network and a Fitting Function

To compare architectures we need a network whose depth and width we can change. make_mlp() builds a stack of Linear -> ReLU -> Dropout blocks from a vector of hidden-layer sizes, so c(32, 16) means two hidden layers with 32 and then 16 units.

make_mlp <- nn_module(
  initialize = function(n_in, hidden, p_drop) {
    layers <- list()
    prev <- n_in
    for (h in hidden) {
      layers <- c(layers, list(nn_linear(prev, h), nn_relu()))
      if (p_drop > 0) layers <- c(layers, list(nn_dropout(p = p_drop)))
      prev <- h
    }
    layers <- c(layers, list(nn_linear(prev, 2)))
    self$net <- do.call(nn_sequential, layers)
  },
  forward = function(x) self$net(x)
)

fit_mlp <- function(hidden, p_drop, wd, lr, class_wt = NULL,
                    max_epochs = 100, seed = 2026) {
  torch_manual_seed(seed)
  loss <- if (is.null(class_wt)) nn_cross_entropy_loss() else nn_cross_entropy_loss(weight = class_wt)

  make_mlp |>
    setup(loss = loss, optimizer = optim_adam) |>
    set_hparams(n_in = n_features, hidden = hidden, p_drop = p_drop) |>
    set_opt_hparams(lr = lr, weight_decay = wd) |>
    fit(train_dl, epochs = max_epochs, valid_data = val_dl, verbose = FALSE,
        callbacks = list(luz_callback_early_stopping(monitor = "valid_loss", patience = 8)),
        accelerator = accelerator(cpu = TRUE))
}

get_probs <- function(fitted, x_t) {
  fitted |>
    predict(x_t, accelerator = accelerator(cpu = TRUE)) |>
    nnf_softmax(dim = 2) |>
    as.matrix()
}

eval_metrics <- function(truth, prob_pos, thr = 0.5) {
  truth <- factor(truth, levels = c(0, 1))
  cls   <- factor(ifelse(prob_pos >= thr, 1, 0), levels = c(0, 1))
  tibble(
    AUC  = roc_auc_vec(truth, prob_pos, event_level = "second"),
    Sens = sens_vec(truth, cls, event_level = "second"),
    Spec = spec_vec(truth, cls, event_level = "second"),
    Acc  = accuracy_vec(truth, cls)
  )
}

Two ideas here that are new relative to ridge/lasso:

  • Early stopping. Training runs for up to 100 epochs, but stops once the validation loss hasn’t improved for 8 epochs in a row. The number of epochs is itself a form of regularization, and this way we don’t have to tune it by hand.
  • Learning rate (lr). This is the step size of the Adam optimizer. Too large and training bounces around; too small and it crawls (and early stopping may quit before it gets anywhere).

2.6 The Tuning Grid

We’ll cross the following choices (40 networks in total):

Hyperparameter Values
Architecture (hidden units) 8, 32, 32-16, 64-32, 64-32-16
Dropout probability 0, 0.3
Weight decay (L2) 0, 1e-3
Learning rate 0.01, 0.001

We rank the models by validation AUC. We use AUC rather than accuracy because CHD is rare and accuracy is dominated by the majority class (more on that below); AUC judges how well the model ranks cases above non-cases, regardless of threshold.

archs <- list(
  "8"        = 8,
  "32"       = 32,
  "32-16"    = c(32, 16),
  "64-32"    = c(64, 32),
  "64-32-16" = c(64, 32, 16)
)

grid <- expand_grid(
  arch   = names(archs),
  p_drop = c(0, 0.3),
  wd     = c(0, 1e-3),
  lr     = c(0.01, 0.001)
)

# The 40-network grid is slow, so the results are saved to disk and reloaded on later
# renders. Delete tune_res.rds to re-run the search (e.g. after changing the grid).
if (file.exists("tune_res.rds")) {
  tune_res <- readRDS("tune_res.rds")
} else {
tune_res <- grid |>
  mutate(res = pmap(list(arch, p_drop, wd, lr), function(arch, p_drop, wd, lr) {
    f <- fit_mlp(archs[[arch]], p_drop, wd, lr)
    p_tr  <- get_probs(f, x_train_t)[, 2]
    p_val <- get_probs(f, x_val_t)[, 2]
    tibble(
      epochs    = length(f$records$metrics$valid),
      train_auc = roc_auc_vec(factor(y_train, levels = c(0, 1)), p_tr,  event_level = "second"),
      val_auc   = roc_auc_vec(factor(y_val,   levels = c(0, 1)), p_val, event_level = "second"),
      val_ll    = mn_log_loss_vec(factor(y_val, levels = c(1, 0)), p_val)
    )
  })) |>
  unnest(res) |>
  arrange(desc(val_auc))
  saveRDS(tune_res, "tune_res.rds")
}
tune_res |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  kbl2(digits = 3, caption = "Top 10 Configurations by Validation AUC")
Top 10 Configurations by Validation AUC
arch p_drop wd lr epochs train_auc val_auc val_ll
8 0.3 0.001 0.001 51 0.757 0.708 0.391
8 0.3 0.000 0.001 51 0.757 0.707 0.391
8 0.3 0.001 0.010 16 0.761 0.707 0.392
64-32-16 0.3 0.001 0.010 10 0.770 0.706 0.397
8 0.0 0.001 0.010 18 0.765 0.706 0.397

tune_res |>
  mutate(reg = paste0("dropout = ", p_drop, ", wd = ", wd),
         lr  = paste("lr =", lr),
         arch = factor(arch, levels = names(archs))) |>
  ggplot(aes(arch, val_auc, colour = reg, group = reg)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) + geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~lr) +
  labs(x = "Architecture (hidden units)", y = "Validation AUC", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

A few things to look for in the table and plot:

  • Train vs. validation AUC. A big gap (train much higher than validation) is overfitting — most likely for the deeper/wider networks with no dropout and no weight decay.
  • Diminishing returns. With ~2,500 training rows and a handful of predictors, we don’t expect big networks to beat small ones by much. Many configurations will be within noise of each other (validation AUC on ~840 rows has a standard error of a couple of points), so prefer the simpler model when it’s a near-tie.
best <- tune_res |> slice_head(n = 1)
best |> kbl2(digits = 3, caption = "Selected Configuration")
Selected Configuration
arch p_drop wd lr epochs train_auc val_auc val_ll
8 0.3 0.001 0.001 51 0.757 0.708 0.391

2.7 Comparison: Random Forest

Before going further with the network, it’s fair to ask whether a neural network is even the right tool here. Random forests are a strong default for tabular data, so we fit one as a benchmark. We use the caret package to choose mtry (the number of predictors tried at each split) by 5-fold cross-validated AUC. To keep things on equal footing with the network, the forest is tuned using only the training set, and we then score it on the validation set.

# caret needs syntactically valid class labels
to_caret <- function(d) mutate(d, TenYearCHD = factor(ifelse(TenYearCHD == 1, "yes", "no"),
                                                     levels = c("no", "yes")))
train_c <- to_caret(train)
val_c   <- to_caret(val)
test_c  <- to_caret(test)

# as above: tune once, save, and reload on later renders (delete rf_fit.rds to refit)
if (file.exists("rf_fit.rds")) {
  rf_fit <- readRDS("rf_fit.rds")
} else {
set.seed(2026)
rf_fit <- caret::train(
  TenYearCHD ~ ., data = train_c,
  method    = "rf",
  ntree     = 500,
  metric    = "ROC",
  tuneGrid  = data.frame(mtry = 1:n_features),
  trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5,
                           classProbs = TRUE, summaryFunction = twoClassSummary)
)
  saveRDS(rf_fit, "rf_fit.rds")
}

rf_fit$bestTune
  mtry
2    2
plot(rf_fit)
p_val_rf <- predict(rf_fit, val_c, type = "prob")[, "yes"]

bind_rows(
  tibble(Model = "Best neural network", Val_AUC = best$val_auc),
  tibble(Model = paste0("Random forest (mtry = ", rf_fit$bestTune$mtry, ")"),
         Val_AUC = eval_metrics(y_val, p_val_rf)$AUC)
) |> kbl2(digits = 3, caption = "Validation AUC: Neural Network vs. Random Forest")

2.8 The Selected Model at the Default Threshold

We refit the selected configuration and look at its validation-set performance using the usual 0.5 cutoff.

fit_best <- fit_mlp(archs[[best$arch]], best$p_drop, best$wd, best$lr)

p_val_best <- get_probs(fit_best, x_val_t)[, 2]
eval_metrics(y_val, p_val_best) |>
  kbl2(digits = 3, caption = "Selected Model: Validation Set, Threshold = 0.5")
Selected Model: Validation Set, Threshold = 0.5
AUC Sens Spec Acc
0.708 0.085 0.995 0.856

What’s causing the low sensitivity? With the default cutoff, accuracy is maximized by saying few people are cases:

table(Predicted_positive = p_val_best > 0.5, Truth = y_val)
                  Truth
Predicted_positive   0   1
             FALSE 645 107
             TRUE    3  10
round(prop.table(table(y_train)), 3)
y_train
    0     1 
0.847 0.153

Note: these proportions do match what is in the data.

We’ll look at two ways to address this, using the selected architecture: first a weighted loss function, and then adjusting the cutoff.

2.9 Fix 1: Weighted Loss

Previously we used no weight = argument, so every training example counts equally. The fastest way to shrink the loss is to push predicted probabilities toward the majority class (“no CHD”) for almost everyone. Weighting each class inversely to its frequency makes a missed case cost far more.

class_weights <- as.numeric(1 / table(y_train))
class_weights <- class_weights / sum(class_weights) * 2
class_weights
[1] 0.3057491 1.6942509
class_weights_t <- torch_tensor(class_weights, dtype = torch_float())

fit_best_wt <- fit_mlp(archs[[best$arch]], best$p_drop, best$wd, best$lr,
                       class_wt = class_weights_t)

p_val_wt <- get_probs(fit_best_wt, x_val_t)[, 2]

bind_rows(
  eval_metrics(y_val, p_val_best) |> mutate(Model = "Selected model"),
  eval_metrics(y_val, p_val_wt)   |> mutate(Model = "Selected model + weighted loss")
) |>
  relocate(Model) |>
  kbl2(digits = 3, caption = "Weighted Loss (Validation Set, Threshold = 0.5)")
Weighted Loss (Validation Set, Threshold = 0.5)
Model AUC Sens Spec Acc
Selected model 0.708 0.085 0.995 0.856
Selected model + weighted loss 0.709 0.641 0.671 0.667

Note we run on the cpu here because of the M1/M2 Mac issue we discussed.

2.10 Fix 2: Threshold Tuning Instead of Reweighting

Weighting the loss changes what the network learns. There’s a cheaper alternative that changes nothing about training: leave the model as fit, and move the classification threshold away from 0.5 at prediction time, using Youden’s \(J = \text{Sens} + \text{Spec} - 1\).

The threshold is a tuning parameter too, so we choose it on the validation set, not the test set. Otherwise the test estimate wouldn’t be honest.

tune_threshold_j <- function(truth, prob, grid = NULL) {
  if (is.null(grid)) grid <- sort(unique(prob))
  truth <- factor(truth, levels = c(0, 1))

  best_t <- 0.5
  best_j <- -Inf
  for (t in grid) {
    cls <- factor(ifelse(prob >= t, 1, 0), levels = c(0, 1))
    se  <- sens_vec(truth, cls, event_level = "second")
    sp  <- spec_vec(truth, cls, event_level = "second")
    j   <- as.numeric(se + sp - 1)
    if (!is.na(j) && j > best_j) {
      best_j <- j
      best_t <- t
    }
  }
  best_t
}

thr_best <- tune_threshold_j(y_val, p_val_best)
thr_wt   <- tune_threshold_j(y_val, p_val_wt)
c(unweighted = thr_best, weighted = thr_wt)
unweighted   weighted 
 0.1161129  0.3696095 
bind_rows(
  eval_metrics(y_val, p_val_best, 0.5)      |> mutate(Model = "Selected", Threshold = "0.5"),
  eval_metrics(y_val, p_val_best, thr_best) |> mutate(Model = "Selected", Threshold = "Youden"),
  eval_metrics(y_val, p_val_wt,   0.5)      |> mutate(Model = "Selected + weighted loss", Threshold = "0.5"),
  eval_metrics(y_val, p_val_wt,   thr_wt)   |> mutate(Model = "Selected + weighted loss", Threshold = "Youden")
) |>
  relocate(Model, Threshold) |>
  kbl2(digits = 3, caption = "Weighting vs. Threshold Tuning (Validation Set)")
Weighting vs. Threshold Tuning (Validation Set)
Model Threshold AUC Sens Spec Acc
Selected 0.5 0.708 0.085 0.995 0.856
Selected Youden 0.708 0.838 0.520 0.569
Selected + weighted loss 0.5 0.709 0.641 0.671 0.667
Selected + weighted loss Youden 0.709 0.855 0.480 0.537
Important

The unweighted model’s Youden threshold comes out well below 0.5, because its predicted probabilities for the positive class are systematically compressed low. This is a prediction-time fix, not a training-time one. Reweighting the loss changes what the network optimizes; threshold tuning changes how we read out an already-fit model. They aren’t mutually exclusive, and the weighted model’s Youden threshold should land much closer to 0.5 since the weighting has already done part of the job. Note that AUC doesn’t change with the threshold. It’s the same model, ranked the same way.

2.11 Honest Error Estimate on the Test Set

Everything above (architecture, hyperparameters, class weights, thresholds) was chosen using the training and validation sets. The test set has not been touched, so we can now report performance for each final strategy, using the thresholds chosen on the validation set.

p_test_best <- get_probs(fit_best,    x_test_t)[, 2]
p_test_wt   <- get_probs(fit_best_wt, x_test_t)[, 2]
p_test_rf   <- predict(rf_fit, test_c, type = "prob")[, "yes"]
thr_rf      <- tune_threshold_j(y_val, p_val_rf)   # threshold chosen on validation

bind_rows(
  eval_metrics(y_test, p_test_best, 0.5)      |> mutate(Model = "Selected", Threshold = "0.5"),
  eval_metrics(y_test, p_test_best, thr_best) |> mutate(Model = "Selected", Threshold = "Youden (from validation)"),
  eval_metrics(y_test, p_test_wt,   0.5)      |> mutate(Model = "Selected + weighted loss", Threshold = "0.5"),
  eval_metrics(y_test, p_test_wt,   thr_wt)   |> mutate(Model = "Selected + weighted loss", Threshold = "Youden (from validation)"),
  eval_metrics(y_test, p_test_rf,   0.5)      |> mutate(Model = "Random forest", Threshold = "0.5"),
  eval_metrics(y_test, p_test_rf,   thr_rf)   |> mutate(Model = "Random forest", Threshold = "Youden (from validation)")
) |>
  relocate(Model, Threshold) |>
  kbl2(digits = 3, caption = "Final Test-Set Performance (never used for any tuning)")
Final Test-Set Performance (never used for any tuning)
Model Threshold AUC Sens Spec Acc
Selected 0.5 0.727 0.026 0.997 0.849
Selected Youden (from validation) 0.727 0.769 0.569 0.599
Selected + weighted loss 0.5 0.728 0.581 0.743 0.718
Selected + weighted loss Youden (from validation) 0.728 0.829 0.538 0.582
Random forest 0.5 0.677 0.034 0.988 0.842
Random forest Youden (from validation) 0.677 0.615 0.599 0.602

Compare these to the validation numbers. The test-set values are the ones to report. The validation values are somewhat optimistic, because we picked the winner from 40 candidates using them. (Here test AUC happens to come out a bit higher than validation AUC, which is just sampling variability in a ~770-row split.) The pattern from validation carries over: at 0.5 the unweighted network catches almost no cases, while weighting or a Youden threshold buys much higher sensitivity at the cost of specificity. The random forest, tuned with caret, has a lower AUC than the networks on both validation and test, and needs the same threshold fix.

Note

This is a single split with a single random initialization per network, so differences of a point or two of AUC between configurations are mostly noise. To be more careful you could use cross-validation for the tuning step, or average over several seeds. We keep it to one split here so it stays fast and easy to follow.

3 Part 2: Cranking It Up — Detecting Pneumonia from Chest X-Rays

3.1 The Data: PneumoniaMNIST

PneumoniaMNIST is a real, public pediatric chest X-ray dataset (from the MedMNIST collection), pre-processed to 28×28 grayscale images with a binary label: normal vs. pneumonia. It ships with its own train/validation/test split, so unlike Part 1 we don’t need to carve one out ourselves.

url <- "https://zenodo.org/records/10519652/files/pneumoniamnist.npz?download=1"
dest_zip <- "pneumoniamnist.npz"

if (!file.exists(dest_zip)) {
  download.file(url, dest_zip, mode = "wb")
}

unzip(dest_zip, list = TRUE)   # confirm the array names inside before loading

The class counts above are imbalanced — pneumonia cases outnumber normal ones in this dataset, the same kind of imbalance we discussed above. We’ll come back to that when we pick a decision threshold.

A quick look at a few images:

par(mfrow = c(3, 3), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
for (i in 1:9) {
  lbl <- ifelse(train_labels[i] == 1, "Pneumonia", "Normal")
  image(t(apply(train_images[i, , ], 2, rev)), col = gray.colors(256),
        axes = FALSE, main = lbl)
}

A normal, aerated lung is mostly air, and air lets X-rays pass through easily — so on a standard chest X-ray, healthy lung tissue shows up as dark (radiolucent), while denser structures (bone, heart, fluid) show up as light/white (radiopaque).

Pneumonia fills the alveoli with fluid, pus, or inflammatory exudate instead of air, so the infected regions attenuate X-rays more than normal lung does. That shows up as patches of increased whiteness/opacity — often called “infiltrates” or “consolidation” — layered on top of what would otherwise be dark lung field. Sometimes you’ll also see it obscure normal landmarks like the heart border or diaphragm edge (“silhouette sign”) where the opacity sits right up against them.

A “pneumonia” image should generally look like it has more light/white patchy or hazy regions within the lung fields than a “normal” image, which should look more uniformly dark where the lungs are. It’s not a simple “more white overall” rule though — bones, the heart, and the mediastinum are white in every chest X-ray regardless of diagnosis; what you’re looking for is unusual whiteness specifically in areas that should be dark lung.

3.2 Is This a Good Problem for a Neural Network?

Reasons it is:

  • Images have spatial structure. A random forest or logistic regression on 784 raw pixels treats each pixel as an unrelated column, discarding the fact that neighbouring pixels form edges and textures. Convolutions are built for exactly this, and the same filter is reused across the image, so the parameter count stays manageable.
  • The signal is a pattern, not a variable. Pneumonia shows up as patchy opacity in certain regions, and no single pixel is informative on its own. Learning features from the raw data is what deep networks do best. There is no obvious hand-made predictor to feed a simpler model.
  • We have thousands of images, far more inputs per observation than in Part 1, and a benchmark dataset with a pre-defined train/validation/test split.

Reasons to be cautious:

  • The images are tiny. At 28×28 much of the fine detail a radiologist would use is gone. Real chest X-ray models work with images of a few hundred pixels per side, and typically start from a pretrained network (transfer learning) rather than training from scratch.
  • Only ~4,700 training images for a model with over 100,000 parameters, so overfitting is a real risk and regularization matters.
  • Generalization and validity. These images come from a single pediatric hospital. A model can pick up scanner, hospital, or patient-population quirks instead of pathology and then fail elsewhere. Good test-set numbers here don’t guarantee that performance will hold in a new setting.
  • Like Part 1, it’s a black box, which is a real concern in a clinical setting.

3.3 Preparing Tensors

prep_images <- function(x) {
  x <- x / 255                                    # scale pixel intensities to [0,1]
  t <- torch_tensor(x, dtype = torch_float())
  t$unsqueeze(2)                                  # (N, H, W) -> (N, 1, H, W): add channel dim
}

x_train_img <- prep_images(train_images)
x_val_img   <- prep_images(val_images)
x_test_img  <- prep_images(test_images)

# +1: torch's cross-entropy loss expects class indices starting at 1
y_train_img <- torch_tensor(as.integer(as.vector(train_labels)) + 1L, dtype = torch_long())
y_val_img   <- torch_tensor(as.integer(as.vector(val_labels))   + 1L, dtype = torch_long())
y_test_img  <- torch_tensor(as.integer(as.vector(test_labels))  + 1L, dtype = torch_long())

train_ds_img <- tensor_dataset(x_train_img, y_train_img)
val_ds_img   <- tensor_dataset(x_val_img,   y_val_img)
test_ds_img  <- tensor_dataset(x_test_img,  y_test_img)

train_dl_img <- dataloader(train_ds_img, batch_size = 64, shuffle = TRUE)
val_dl_img   <- dataloader(val_ds_img,   batch_size = 64, shuffle = FALSE)
test_dl_img  <- dataloader(test_ds_img,  batch_size = 64, shuffle = FALSE)

3.4 A Convolutional Neural Network

Every network so far in this course has been a stack of dense (fully connected) layers — for images, that means flattening the picture into a long vector and throwing away all spatial structure. A convolutional layer instead slides small learned filters across the image, picking up local patterns (edges, textures) wherever they occur; a pooling layer then downsamples, making the representation smaller and more robust to small shifts in position. Stacking a few of these is what makes CNNs the standard architecture for image data.

Link to video explaining CNNs.

torch_manual_seed(2026)

cnn_net <- nn_module(
  initialize = function() {
    self$conv1   <- nn_conv2d(in_channels = 1,  out_channels = 16, kernel_size = 3, padding = 1)
    self$conv2   <- nn_conv2d(in_channels = 16, out_channels = 32, kernel_size = 3, padding = 1)
    self$pool    <- nn_max_pool2d(kernel_size = 2)
    self$dropout <- nn_dropout(p = 0.3)
    self$fc1     <- nn_linear(32 * 7 * 7, 64)
    self$fc2     <- nn_linear(64, 2)
  },
  forward = function(x) {
    x <- x |> self$conv1() |> nnf_relu() |> self$pool()   # 28x28 -> 14x14
    x <- x |> self$conv2() |> nnf_relu() |> self$pool()   # 14x14 -> 7x7
    x <- x$reshape(c(x$size(1), -1))                      # flatten for the dense layers
    x <- x |> self$dropout() |> self$fc1() |> nnf_relu() |> self$dropout() |> self$fc2()
    x
  }
)

3.4.1 What Each Piece Does, and Why We Chose It

Convolutional layers: nn_conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size, padding)

A convolutional layer slides a small window of learned weights (a filter) across the image. At each position it takes a weighted sum of the pixels under the window, producing one number in an output grid called a feature map. Each option controls one aspect of this:

  • in_channels: how many maps the layer receives. conv1 sees the raw image, which is grayscale, so this is 1 (a color photo would be 3). conv2 receives conv1’s output, so it must be 16.
  • out_channels: how many different filters the layer learns, and therefore how many feature maps it outputs. Each filter tends to specialize in a different pattern, such as an edge at a particular angle or a bright patch. More filters means more patterns but more parameters and computation. We use 16, then 32. The usual convention is to increase the number of filters as the image shrinks. Early layers detect a small set of simple patterns (edges, gradients), while later layers combine them into many more complex ones (textures, shapes such as a hazy region next to the heart border), so more channels are useful deeper in. With only 28×28 inputs and ~4,700 training images, a modest 16/32 keeps the network small enough to train on a laptop CPU and limits overfitting.
  • kernel_size = 3: the filter is a 3×3 window. Small kernels are the modern default: two stacked 3×3 layers see a 5×5 region but use fewer parameters than one 5×5 layer, and they add an extra nonlinearity. On a 28×28 image, larger kernels would cover a big fraction of the picture and wouldn’t capture “local” structure. Each filter in conv1 has only 3×3×1 + 1 = 10 parameters, and the same weights are reused at every position, which is why convolutions are so parameter-efficient.
  • padding = 1: adds a one-pixel border of zeros before sliding the filter. Without it a 3×3 window can’t be centered on edge pixels, and each convolution would trim the image from 28×28 to 26×26. With padding = 1 the output has the same height and width as the input (for a 3×3 kernel), so all of the shrinking in the network comes from the pooling layers, which keeps the size bookkeeping simple.

ReLU activation: nnf_relu()

After each convolution (and after fc1) we apply ReLU, \(\max(0, x)\). Without a nonlinearity between layers, a stack of convolutions and linear layers would collapse into a single linear operation, no matter how many we stacked. ReLU is the default choice because it is cheap to compute and doesn’t squash large values the way sigmoid/tanh do, which makes deep networks much easier to train. It has no parameters to tune.

Pooling: nn_max_pool2d(kernel_size = 2)

Max pooling looks at each non-overlapping 2×2 block of a feature map and keeps only the largest value. This halves the height and width (28×28 → 14×14 → 7×7), so each later layer has a quarter as many positions to process. It also makes the representation tolerant of small shifts, since a pattern that moves by a pixel often still produces the same maximum. It is useful for us because a pneumonia opacity can appear in slightly different places from image to image. Keeping the maximum (rather than the average) says “was this pattern detected anywhere in this block?” The pooling layer has no learned weights, and we reuse one pool object for both stages. A 2×2 window is standard: bigger windows throw away spatial information too quickly on such a small image.

Flattening: x$reshape(c(x$size(1), -1))

The dense layers expect one long vector per image, not a stack of maps. This line keeps the batch dimension (x$size(1)) and lets torch (-1) work out the rest, turning each (32, 7, 7) block into a vector of 32 × 7 × 7 = 1,568 numbers.

Dense layers: nn_linear(in_features, out_features)

A fully connected layer: every input number connects to every output unit, with its own weight. The earlier layers extract features and the dense layers use those features to make the decision.

  • fc1 = nn_linear(32 * 7 * 7, 64): in_features must exactly match the flattened size (1,568), or torch will throw a shape error. This is why the padding and pooling arithmetic above matters. The 64 hidden units are a judgment call: enough capacity to combine the 1,568 features into a useful summary, but not so many that this one layer (which already holds more than 100,000 weights) dominates and overfits. Powers of two such as 32, 64, 128 are conventional (they are efficient on hardware), and nothing magic distinguishes 64 from, say, 50. Like the filters, this is a hyperparameter you would ideally tune on the validation set, as we did for the Framingham network.
  • fc2 = nn_linear(64, 2): the output layer has one unit per class (normal, pneumonia), so out_features = 2. It has no ReLU after it because it should output unbounded scores (“logits”). nn_cross_entropy_loss() applies the softmax internally during training, and we apply nnf_softmax() ourselves at prediction time to convert the scores to probabilities.

Putting the sizes together

Step Output shape (per image)
Input 1 × 28 × 28
conv1 + ReLU 16 × 28 × 28
pool 16 × 14 × 14
conv2 + ReLU 32 × 14 × 14
pool 32 × 7 × 7
flatten 1,568
fc1 + ReLU 64
fc2 2

This is a deliberately small, classic design (two conv/pool stages followed by a small dense head), in the spirit of early networks like LeNet. It is a reasonable starting point for 28×28 images, not a tuned optimum. Depth, filter counts, and the width of fc1 could all be compared on the validation set in the same way we compared architectures in Part 1.

model_inst <- cnn_net()

# Show the architecture
print(model_inst)
An `nn_module` containing 105,346 parameters.

── Modules ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• conv1: <nn_conv2d> #160 parameters
• conv2: <nn_conv2d> #4,640 parameters
• pool: <nn_max_pool2d> #0 parameters
• dropout: <nn_dropout> #0 parameters
• fc1: <nn_linear> #100,416 parameters
• fc2: <nn_linear> #130 parameters
## "Neurons" per layer — for the dense layers this is unambiguous (layer width);
## for the conv layers, the closest analogue is the number of output channels
## (filters), since each filter is scanned across every spatial position.
tibble(
  Layer   = c("conv1", "conv2", "fc1", "fc2"),
  Neurons = c(16, 32, 64, 2)   # out_channels for conv layers, out_features for linear layers
) |> kbl2(caption = "Neurons (Output Channels / Units) per Layer")
Neurons (Output Channels / Units) per Layer
Layer Neurons
conv1 16
conv2 32
fc1 64
fc2 2

The conv layers look “small” (16, 32 filters) next to fc1’s 64 units, but they’re doing far more work per parameter — each of those 16 (then 32) filters gets applied at every position in the image, producing a 16 × 28 × 28 (then 32 × 14 × 14) stack of activations, even though the filter itself only has a handful of weights (3×3×in_channels + 1 bias each).

## Per-layer parameter counts
params <- model_inst$named_parameters()

param_tbl <- tibble(
  Layer    = names(params),
  Shape    = sapply(params, function(p) paste(dim(p), collapse = " x ")),
  N_Params = sapply(params, function(p) p$numel())
)

param_tbl |> kbl2(caption = "CNN Parameters by Layer")
CNN Parameters by Layer
Layer Shape N_Params
conv1.weight 16 x 1 x 3 x 3 144
conv1.bias 16 16
conv2.weight 32 x 16 x 3 x 3 4608
conv2.bias 32 32
fc1.weight 64 x 1568 100352
fc1.bias 64 64
fc2.weight 2 x 64 128
fc2.bias 2 2 
## Total trainable parameters
sum(param_tbl$N_Params)
[1] 105346

Almost all the trainable parameters will be sitting in fc1 (32 × 7 × 7 = 1568 inputs into 64 units is over 100,000 weights) — worth pointing out that flattening right before the dense layers is usually where a CNN’s parameter count balloons, not in the conv layers themselves.

Since pneumonia cases outnumber normal cases in training, we weight the loss so the rarer class isn’t effectively ignored — the same spirit as the cost-sensitive thresholds we used for Naive Bayes, applied during training instead of afterward.

class_counts  <- table(as.integer(as.vector(train_labels)))
class_weights <- as.numeric(1 / class_counts)
class_weights <- class_weights / sum(class_weights) * 2   # normalize, 2 classes
class_weights_t <- torch_tensor(class_weights, dtype = torch_float())

class_weights
[1] 1.4842821 0.5157179
# Fitted torch/luz objects can't be cached by knitr, so we cache by hand:
# train once, save to disk with luz_save(), and reload on later renders.
# (Delete cnn_fit.luz to force a retrain.)
if (file.exists("cnn_fit.luz")) {
  fitted_cnn <- luz_load("cnn_fit.luz")
} else {
  fitted_cnn <- cnn_net |>
    setup(
      loss      = nn_cross_entropy_loss(weight = class_weights_t),
      optimizer = optim_adam,
      metrics   = list(luz_metric_accuracy())
    ) |>
    set_opt_hparams(lr = 0.001, weight_decay = 1e-4) |>
    fit(train_dl_img, epochs = 15, valid_data = val_dl_img, verbose = TRUE,
        accelerator = accelerator(cpu = TRUE))
  luz_save(fitted_cnn, "cnn_fit.luz")
}

plot(fitted_cnn)

weight_decay = 1e-4 is the same L2 regularization idea from Part 1 — here it’s earning its keep, since this CNN has far more parameters relative to its ~4,700 training images than the tabular network did.

3.5 A Non-Neural Alternative: A Smooth Coefficient Surface

Before crediting the CNN for everything, let’s try a classical method that also respects the 2D structure of the image. A logistic regression on the raw pixels would have 784 coefficients, one per pixel, with no notion that neighbouring pixels are related. Instead we can require the coefficients to form a smooth surface over the image grid:

\[ \text{logit}\, P(\text{pneumonia}) = \beta_0 + \sum_{r,c} \beta(r, c)\, x_{rc}, \qquad \beta(r, c) = \sum_{j} \theta_j\, B_j(r, c), \]

where \(B_j(r, c)\) are the basis functions of a 2D tensor-product spline (the same kind of smooth you would get from te() in mgcv, from our splines/GAM lectures). Substituting, the model becomes an ordinary logistic regression on the \(k^2 - 1\) scores \(z_j = \sum_{r,c} B_j(r,c)\, x_{rc}\), which are just a matrix multiplication of the images by the basis. So the “hard” part is only building the basis once.

The number of knots per dimension, \(k\), controls how wiggly the coefficient surface can be, and it is the tuning parameter. We pick it on the validation set, exactly as we did with the network architecture.

library(mgcv)

# flatten each 28x28 image into a row; column order is (row fastest), matching `grid` below
flatten <- function(a) matrix(a / 255, nrow = dim(a)[1])
X_tr <- flatten(train_images)
X_va <- flatten(val_images)
X_te <- flatten(test_images)

y_tr <- as.integer(as.vector(train_labels))
y_va <- as.integer(as.vector(val_labels))

# pixel coordinates, with row index varying fastest to match the flattening above
pix_grid <- expand.grid(r = (1:28) / 28, c = (1:28) / 28)

# tensor-product P-spline basis evaluated at every pixel: a 784 x (k^2 - 1) matrix
spline_basis <- function(k) {
  smoothCon(te(r, c, bs = "ps", k = c(k, k)), data = pix_grid, absorb.cons = TRUE)[[1]]$X
}

fit_spline_lr <- function(k) {
  B <- spline_basis(k)
  Z <- X_tr %*% B; colnames(Z) <- paste0("b", seq_len(ncol(B)))
  list(B = B, fit = glm(y ~ ., data = data.frame(y = y_tr, Z), family = binomial))
}

predict_spline_lr <- function(m, X) {
  Z <- X %*% m$B; colnames(Z) <- paste0("b", seq_len(ncol(m$B)))
  as.numeric(predict(m$fit, data.frame(Z), type = "response"))
}

spline_fits <- map(c(4, 6, 8, 10, 12), fit_spline_lr)

spline_tune <- tibble(
  k         = c(4, 6, 8, 10, 12),
  n_coef    = map_int(spline_fits, ~ ncol(.x$B)),
  train_auc = map_dbl(spline_fits, ~ eval_metrics(y_tr, predict_spline_lr(.x, X_tr))$AUC),
  val_auc   = map_dbl(spline_fits, ~ eval_metrics(y_va, predict_spline_lr(.x, X_va))$AUC)
)

spline_tune |> kbl2(digits = 3, caption = "Spline Logistic Regression: Choosing the Number of Knots (k) on the Validation Set")
Spline Logistic Regression: Choosing the Number of Knots (k) on the Validation Set
k n_coef train_auc val_auc
4 15 0.965 0.960
6 35 0.986 0.986
8 63 0.989 0.987
10 99 0.992 0.990
12 143 0.994 0.989 
best_k      <- spline_tune$k[which.max(spline_tune$val_auc)]
spline_best <- spline_fits[[which(spline_tune$k == best_k)]]

# the estimated coefficient surface beta(r, c) = B %*% theta
beta_surface <- matrix(spline_best$B %*% coef(spline_best$fit)[-1], nrow = 28)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
image(t(apply(beta_surface, 2, rev)), axes = FALSE,
      col = hcl.colors(50, "Blue-Red 3"),
      main = paste0("Estimated coefficient surface (k = ", best_k, ")"))

Red regions are where brighter pixels push the prediction toward pneumonia, and blue regions are where they push toward normal. This is the interpretability advantage over the CNN: the whole model is a single picture.

3.5.1 Head-to-Head on the Test Set

Both models choose their classification threshold on the validation set using Youden’s index, and the test set is used once.

p_val_cnn  <- fitted_cnn |>
  predict(x_val_img, accelerator = accelerator(cpu = TRUE)) |>
  nnf_softmax(dim = 2) |> as.matrix()
p_val_cnn  <- p_val_cnn[, 2]

p_test_cnn <- fitted_cnn |>
  predict(x_test_img) |>
  nnf_softmax(dim = 2) |>
  as.matrix()

p_pneumonia <- p_test_cnn[, 2]

p_val_spl  <- predict_spline_lr(spline_best, X_va)
p_test_spl <- predict_spline_lr(spline_best, X_te)

thr_cnn <- tune_threshold_j(y_va, p_val_cnn)
thr_spl <- tune_threshold_j(y_va, p_val_spl)

truth_test  <- as.integer(as.vector(test_labels))

bind_rows(
  eval_metrics(truth_test, p_pneumonia) |> mutate(Threshold = 0.5, Model = "CNN"),
  eval_metrics(truth_test, p_pneumonia, thr_cnn) |> mutate(Threshold = thr_cnn, Model = "CNN"),
  eval_metrics(truth_test, p_test_spl) |> mutate(Threshold = 0.5, Model = paste0("Spline logistic regression (k = ", best_k, ")")),
  eval_metrics(truth_test, p_test_spl,  thr_spl) |> mutate(Threshold = thr_spl, Model = paste0("Spline logistic regression (k = ", best_k, ")"))
) |>
  relocate(Model, Threshold) |>
  kbl2(digits = 3, caption = "Test-Set Performance (Youden threshold chosen on validation)")
Test-Set Performance (Youden threshold chosen on validation)
Model Threshold AUC Sens Spec Acc
CNN 0.500 0.939 0.964 0.778 0.894
CNN 0.278 0.939 0.979 0.726 0.885
Spline logistic regression (k = 10) 0.500 0.919 0.985 0.624 0.849
Spline logistic regression (k = 10) 0.641 0.919 0.982 0.675 0.867

The point of this comparison is not that one method must win. A smooth linear surface on the image is a much more constrained model than a CNN (it can only detect “more or less brightness here”), so it’s informative to see how close it gets. It’s also easy to fit, has one tuning parameter, and yields a coefficient map a clinician can look at. Where the CNN can do better is when the signal isn’t a simple brightness pattern, for example when the shape or texture matters regardless of where it appears. If the two are close, the simpler model is often the better choice.

table(p_pneumonia >= 0.5, p_test_spl >= 0.5)
       
        FALSE TRUE
  FALSE   148   48
  TRUE      4  424
Important

As with the Naive Bayes screening example, think about which error costs more here: missing a real pneumonia case (false negative) is clinically worse than flagging a normal X-ray for review (false positive). If sensitivity at the default 0.5 threshold looks lower than you’d want for a screening tool, that’s the same threshold-shifting exercise from earlier in the course — lowering the cutoff trades some specificity for higher sensitivity.

3.6 A Look at a Few Predictions

set.seed(123)

idx <- unique(c(1,3,4,which((p_pneumonia >= 0.5) & truth_test == 0 )[1:3], 
         which((p_test_spl >= 0.5) & truth_test == 0 )[4:6], 
         which((p_pneumonia >= 0.5) != (p_test_spl >= 0.5))[1:4]
         ))
         

par(mfrow = c(4, 3), mar = c(1, 1, 5, 1))
for (i in idx) {
  true_lbl <- ifelse(truth_test[i] == 1, "Pneumonia", "Normal")
  pred_lbl <- ifelse(p_pneumonia[i] >= 0.5, "Pneumonia", "Normal")
  pred_lbl2 <- ifelse(p_test_spl[i] >= 0.5, "Pneumonia", "Normal")
  image(t(apply(test_images[i, , ], 2, rev)), col = gray.colors(256), axes = FALSE,
        main = paste0("True: ", true_lbl, "\nPred CNN: ", pred_lbl, "\nPred Spl: ", pred_lbl2))
}

4 Summary

  • Weight decay (an L2 penalty built into the optimizer) and dropout are the neural-network analogues of ridge regression and random feature removal — but they mostly matter when the network has real capacity to overfit. On a small tabular network, regularizing barely changed anything; on a CNN with far more parameters relative to its training data, it’s doing real work.
  • Convolutional layers are the first architecture in this course that isn’t just a stack of dense layers — they exploit the spatial structure of image data instead of flattening it away.
  • The same practical themes from earlier in the semester carry over directly to deep learning: class imbalance (handled here with a weighted loss instead of resampling), and cost-sensitive thresholds (the same screening-vs-confirmation logic applies to a CNN’s output probabilities exactly as it did to Naive Bayes).
